analysis.one_liner: Bans US gasoline exports whenever average gas prices stay at or above a set threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, has sat in the House Foreign Affairs Committee since April 2026 with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the President to prohibit exports of gasoline produced in the United States whenever the national average pump price has been at or above $3.12 per gallon for seven straight days, and to lift the ban only after prices fall below that level for seven straight days [S2][S3]. The idea is to keep more gasoline on the domestic market during price spikes. The President could exempt specific exports he deems consistent with the national interest [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers, who would see more of the US gasoline supply reserved for the domestic market during periods when prices spike above the trigger level. Lower-income households, who spend a larger share of their budgets on fuel, would benefit most from any price relief.

how_it_helps.text: The bill automatically triggers an export ban whenever the average US gasoline price has been at or above $3.12 per gallon for seven consecutive days, and ends it only after prices stay below that level for seven consecutive days [S2][S3].
Keeping gasoline that would otherwise be exported adds to domestic supply during price spikes, which puts downward pressure on pump prices for consumers.
The President can exempt individual exports deemed consistent with the national interest, giving flexibility for allies or supply disruptions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US refiners and gasoline exporters, who would lose the ability to sell gasoline abroad during high-price periods — precisely when export margins are most profitable. Foreign buyers of US gasoline would also lose access during those windows.

drawbacks.text: Gasoline prices are set in a global market, and the US is a large exporter of refined products; cutting off exports may not lower domestic prices by much, and some economists argue it could raise them if refiners cut back processing or pass lost export revenue to domestic buyers [S3].

The $3.12 trigger is a fixed number that does not adjust for inflation or regional differences, and the broad presidential exemption authority could allow administrations to waive the ban so often that it rarely binds [S3].
A recurring export ban could discourage investment in US refining capacity and invite retaliation from trading partners against other US exports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real pain point — pump prices — with a simple, automatic mechanism, but its effectiveness is genuinely uncertain. Gasoline markets are regional and global, so an export ban may deliver less relief than sponsors hope, and the fixed price trigger and presidential exemption carve-outs could blunt the policy. It is a consumer-focused idea with real design questions, not a giveaway to any industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee in April 2026, where it has had no further action; the Congress is still in session, so it could still move.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Gasoline Export Ban Act of 2026 on April 14, 2026 [S1][S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs the day it was introduced, and the complete action history shows no hearings, markup, or floor vote since [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached. Refiners and gasoline exporters are better off as long as the bill stays inactive, since their export business continues unrestricted. Drivers gain nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Refiners, while the bill sits dormant

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban gasoline exports during high-price periods and referred it to committee

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has taken no action on the bill since April 2026

sides.party_line_note: Only one member sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored it, so the record shows no partisan split either way [S4].

industries.note: The bill would shut off their most profitable export window — high US prices usually mean high world prices — costing them revenue during exactly the periods the bill targets [S2][S3].
Drivers would get more domestic supply reserved for them during price spikes, though the size of the price relief is debated.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action in months, the bill is following the path of most single-sponsor proposals: it will likely sit in committee and die when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless it is attached to a larger bill or gas prices spike enough to build support quickly.
